exercises.name: Wrist warm up
cues: Build your own from the wrist warm up library, exercises that feel good
Start with 5-10 reps each and experiment
Load management: start with a little weight in the hands, build gradually to full body weight
Take as long as you need (some need a couple of minutes, some more than ten)
Extra care in one arm work: a single wrist starts taking double the weight
mistakes: Rushing the warm up
Loading a full handstand before the wrists are ready

exercises.name: Wall tuck bail
cues: Step up chest facing the wall, knees can bend
Only as high as comfortable, up to about 90 deg
Stay tucked and low; come down by stepping the hand, then each foot (hand, foot, foot)
High reps, one side only, so it becomes an automatic response

exercises.name: Wall tuck hold
cues: Only once comfortable coming down
Tuck plank position, hold, elevate through the shoulders
Progress by bringing the hands closer to the wall

exercises.name: Cartwheel bail (terrible cartwheel)
cues: Start an arm's length from the wall, face away, hands on the floor directly beneath you
Walk the feet up the wall, straight arms the whole time, look at the floor between the hands
Pause at the highest comfortable point, then step one hand forward with a slight inward rotation; that hand brakes and guides the legs
Let the legs drop to one side, same side leg as the moving hand lands first, one foot at a time
Smooth and quiet landing; train one side only (the most natural one)
Keep repeating the same distance until smooth, then move the feet up first, then the hands, closer to the wall
Use a floor marker for the bail distance and decrease it a cm or two per session
mistakes: Pushing or kicking off the wall
Moving closer before the current distance is comfortable
Early faults that are OK: feet landing between you and the wall, wrong foot first, both feet together

exercises.name: Split leg balance (chest to wall)
cues: Prerequisite: comfortable bail from a chest to wall handstand with hands about 30 cm from the wall
Walk up chest to wall, shift weight into the hands, slowly bring one foot away from the wall
Goal heavy to light: lighten the wall foot until all weight is in the hands and balance is in the fingers
Toe tap the wall instead of falling; count toe taps to track progress
Falling before 20 s = the set does not count (when the sheet sets 20 s+)
mistakes: Bringing the feet together
Letting the near-wall foot float away

exercises.name: Wall split leg hold
cues: One toe on the wall at all times
Look at the floor between the hands
Push hold time but keep enough energy to bail

exercises.name: Heel pulls
cues: Kick up back to wall (one of the few back to wall drills), hands about a palm's distance from the wall
Push into your best line, lock the body, push only with the fingertips to lever the heels off the wall
Aim is not to hold but to push off the wall with just the fingers; gaze at the floor
Scale by hand distance from the wall in tiny steps: closer = easier, further = harder
mistakes: Kicking or moving the feet off the wall
Bringing the top leg down on the back to wall kick up
Hands too close to the wall, bouncing back off it

exercises.name: Heel pulls to hold
cues: Back to wall, push into the fingers to lift away and hold as long as possible
Controlled heel pull; count only best-attempt reps
Hands closer to the wall = easier, further = much harder
mistakes: Kicking off the wall

exercises.name: Toe pulls to hold
cues: Chest to wall, push into the heels of the hands to lift off and hold
Count only best-attempt reps
mistakes: Kicking off the wall

exercises.name: Alignment hold (chest to wall)
cues: Focus on alignment, check with video
Chest to wall hold at least 20 s per set

exercises.name: Chest to wall hold
cues: Feet, hips and upper chest touching the wall; hips over shoulders over hands
Push tall, keep elevation, keep pressing into the floor; re-push when you catch yourself sinking
As a warm up: assess how you feel and check position, not an endurance set
As a finisher: push how long you hold form; use a timer
If you cannot hold 60 s on the wall you will not hold 60 s freestanding
mistakes: Making it a balancing drill (keep the feet on the wall)
Sinking out of shoulder elevation

exercises.name: Basic kick up
cues: Swing the arms in from underneath and place the hands at the same time as you kick up
Kick up with split legs; stay in split leg when kicking up
Reach further than you think (test whether this cue works for you)
50/50 rule: for every kick that falls back to the feet, have one that falls over the top
Press with the fingers like brakes to catch in the middle, then gather into the target shape
3 kick ups a set; no balance in 3 attempts = rest; same leg, same spot, same orientation each time
mistakes: Floating to the top with no corrections then sinking back
Always falling to the same side (never finding equilibrium)
Changing the entry each attempt (adds variables)

exercises.name: Top end isolations
cues: Start from a wall or box, top leg as in your basic kick up
Lift the lower leg and shift the weight until the lower foot floats up; do not kick
Arms come underneath, stack on top of the shoulders, maintain split leg, find balance then gather the feet
As many as possible before falling, minimum 3 to count the set
Later: bring the feet together slowly, film to check they gather equally
mistakes: Kicking

exercises.name: 5 second game
cues: Build to a 5 s handstand in 5 kick ups: kick 1 = 1 s, kick 2 = 2 s ... kick 5 = 5 s
Fall over, fail to land on the feet, or miss the hold = back to 1
Must hit 5 feet-together handstands in a row (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 s) to finish
Added challenge: play with a friend, first to 5 s wins

exercises.name: Freestanding split leg hold
cues: Freestanding from the basic kick up
Pin the legs, focus on rebalancing with the fingers

exercises.name: Straddle hold
cues: Jump into straddle or move from split leg, try both
See 4 kick ups you should know (kick up to straddle)

exercises.name: Full (straight) hold
cues: Balance in split leg, then gather the feet; timer starts when the feet are together
Balance is still found in split leg
Do not worry about the line until you can hold at least 40 s (unless it causes pain)

exercises.name: Full to tuck hold
cues: Shoulders try to close as you tuck: elevate and keep them open
Only as low as you can hold (maybe 90 deg at first)

exercises.name: Level 1 shape change
cues: One level 1 change for reps, then rest; can change each session
Quality over quantity
Rotate through all level 1 changes

exercises.name: Level 1 and 2 shape change
cues: A different change from the previous set
Work level 1 weaknesses, add level 2 (suggest tuck)

exercises.name: Level 2 shape and hold
cues: Move into the level 2 shape and hold it 5-10 s
Can LIGHTLY use the wall at first

exercises.name: Tuck hold
cues: Jump into tuck or transition from any kick up; freestanding
Upper back works: keep scapula elevation and shoulder flexion, shoulders over hands
Progress by longer holds and a deeper tuck
Wall toe taps allowed at first, aim freestanding (intermediate)
mistakes: Mechanical tuck: arching the spine and pushing the sternum out instead of elevating
Planching forwards to compensate for lack of shoulder flexion or upper back strength

exercises.name: Wall tuck slides
cues: Chest to wall about 30 cm away, slide the feet down the wall into tuck, using the wall as a guide
Use the wall as little as possible over time, weight and some balance in the hands
As deep as possible, push tall as the shoulders close
Not about speed; intensify with depth, reps or bottom pauses
mistakes: Leaning into the wall, taking pressure off the shoulders

exercises.name: Tuck slides
cues: Too easy = slower tempo or longer pauses
Ultimate tuck = thighs touching ribs, knees together

exercises.name: Basic kick up and hold
cues: Collect 10 holds over the day, each at least PB / 3 (e.g. PB 21 s -> each hold at least 7 s)
Kick up anywhere; go for a max hold each time

exercises.name: Freestanding max hold
cues: Kick up split leg, gather, hold full; max hold while fresh
Fight for balance as long as you can, even past the target
Film the holds
mistakes: Giving up the save too early

exercises.name: Free shape changing
cues: Move between shapes continually for the set time
Include the hard ones

exercises.name: Level 3 shape change
cues: Lowering into 7 is usually easier than lifting into 7
Heavily underbalanced: you will often land back on your feet; the 50/50 rule matters less

exercises.name: Single/double leg seven lifts
cues: Start on a high surface (hip height or higher)
Lift so the toes float off by articulating the spine and pressing into the floor
Only start once the tuck is controlled; single leg 7 first, then double leg 7

exercises.name: Freestanding hold
cues: Warm up check: how you feel, warm up more if needed
20 s+ to count (where stated)

exercises.name: Full to tuck to full
cues: Control, not speed
Bend hips and knees together into the tuck; big centre of mass change

exercises.name: Single/double leg 7 hold
cues: Film to see when you are horizontal (often lower than you think)
Progress from single leg to double leg 7

exercises.name: Press handstand negative (freestanding)
cues: Kick into straddle, pull the legs into the body, slowly round the spine, fight the forward lean
Lower as slowly as possible, smooth throughout (sheet: e.g. 10 s eccentric)
Rough guide: if you can lower over 30 s you could lift it
Dropping at the bottom = lower to blocks and reduce the height over time to reach the floor
Stop the session early if two consecutive reps lower in less than half the time of the first
Expect strong muscle soreness (DOMS) at first
mistakes: Collapsing forward instead of fighting the lean
Using a wall or spotter to block the lean

exercises.name: Head looking at toes (HLAT) hold
cues: Stack high with the traps and shift weight toward the fingers first
Bring the head through in one quick fluid motion (do not move it slowly)
Self-check: see hips and toes together = decent stack; cannot see hips = too piked; cannot see toes = hips too far forward
Upper back must work harder (more underbalance)
mistakes: Moving the head slowly

exercises.name: HLAT full to tuck
cues: Basic kick up, transition to tuck, balance, then change gaze to HLAT (knees here)
Staying HLAT, goal = full to tuck repeated

exercises.name: HLAT full to single/double leg 7
cues: Toward the HLAT 7 milestone
HLAT 7 = one of the most advanced two arm shapes, prerequisite for one arm

exercises.name: HLAT tuck to HLAT full
cues: In and out of tuck to full while looking at the toes, as many as possible

exercises.name: Fast all-level shape changing
cues: Move as fast as possible into different positions; change direction, speed and intensity
Force drastic corrections and fight to stay up; final set is your own routine

exercises.name: Flags chest to wall
cues: Quality, not depth (sheet C); use a box or chairs to measure depth
Always return to centre
Depth version (sheet E): feels like strength, use an object lower down as a target

exercises.name: Freestanding flags
cues: Start in a two arm straddle, fix the straddle, move slowly, crunch into your side to tilt into the flag
Close the gap between the thigh and the side of the body
Pause briefly in straddle between each flag
Quality and depth; toes to floor is a long-term goal with flexibility training
mistakes: Drifting the shoulder out to make the shift instead of bringing the bottom leg down
Dropping the foot into a pike

exercises.name: Chest to wall press negative
cues: Find the right distance from the wall for your straddle; needs wall space

exercises.name: Press from blocks
cues: Start at a height you could do on your worst day (maybe hip height at first)
Lower little by little each session; fail a height 3 times = go back up one
Prerequisite: a solid straddle handstand and consistent straddle to full transition
Push tall: shoulders to the ears; rock onto the toes, open the legs, roll the spine
mistakes: Blocking the shoulders (wall, spotter) so you never resist the lean yourself

exercises.name: Press walks
cues: Quality over quantity, reset each rep
Start with forward walks; once all sets are clean replace early sets with backward walks until all are backward
Use the feet as little as possible; push, do not sink forward with the shoulders

exercises.name: Press negative from blocks (weak link)

cues: Rock up onto the toes, open the legs, roll the spine while opening the shoulders, reach straddle handstand
Push tall throughout: scapular elevation is the platform

exercises.name: Trap-3 raise (unilateral, supported)
cues: Retract and depress the scapula, maintain depression, lift the arm overhead and up, reset the scapula every rep
Weaker side first, then match on the strong side; never more on the strong side
Arm must at least cover the ear
Most start with a 2-4 kg dumbbell; small (0.25 kg) increments help

exercises.name: Trap-1 raise (unilateral, supported)
cues: Same set up as trap-3 but elevate and protract the scapula: up and forward

exercises.name: DB front / planche raise

Lower and stop before the bottom to keep tension

mistakes: Going too heavy and swinging

cues: From two arm straddle shift to about 75% base hand / 25% assisting hand

exercises.name: Fingertip support hold
cues: Push the base hand to lift higher rather than bending and lifting the assisting hand

exercises.name: One arm handstand
cues: Push harder / taller (most common OAHS mistake is not pushing high enough)

fear_of_falling.name: Loading the wrists
fear_of_falling.what: Wrist warm ups, gradually more weight, then a wall tuck hold. Goal: just support the body on the arms and get used to the wall.

fear_of_falling.name: Hand, foot, foot
fear_of_falling.what: Wall tuck bail: stay tucked and low, get up on the wall, come down by stepping the hand, then each foot. High reps, one side only, so it becomes automatic.

fear_of_falling.name: Cartwheel bail
fear_of_falling.what: Progress toward a chest to wall bail: extend the legs first, bail with straight legs, hands one step closer, walk in with the hands, tipping point, bail from chest to wall. Do not go closer or higher until that height is comfortable.
fear_of_falling.measure: Bail distance from the wall in cm (floor marker), decreased fractionally each session (a cm or two)

fear_of_falling.name: Tipping point
fear_of_falling.what: At about 30 cm from the wall the feet must go over or to the side, not between hands and wall: twist and cartwheel out, the hand guiding the feet round. Step back a distance if fear returns; rehearse the twist where comfortable.

fear_of_falling.name: Reactive not proactive
fear_of_falling.what: Chest to wall bail: instead of choosing to fall, try to balance chest to wall (even a split second); when you overbalance by accident, bail reactively. Effectively a freestanding bail.

fear_of_falling.name: First freestanding bail
fear_of_falling.what: Only new part is the kick up. Mission is not to hold: kick with more and more power until you just tip over the top; repeat until it is not scary.

fear_of_falling.name: The 50/50 rule
fear_of_falling.what: Go into overbalance for every time you fall back in underbalance. Most people play it too safe; be brave. You learn how hard to kick to get the centre of mass over the hands.
fear_of_falling.measure: Overbalance falls vs underbalance falls, aiming at about 50:50

fear_of_falling.name: Sticking the handstand (heel pulls)
fear_of_falling.what: Learn how long you can wait before bailing; push with the fingers to slow the momentum and catch it. Heel pulls (the only back to wall drill) teach maximal finger push and wrist flexion strength.

rules.reading: Notation as MFTK: A/B/C order; same letter with numbers (A1/A2) = circuit with rest between each; set ranges to self-regulate; '10+' = expected minimum; upper bound: raise intensity only once the upper limit is hit on all sets; AMRAP over a time period; 4-digit tempo = lower, bottom pause, lift, top pause (X = explosive, '-' = phase absent, C = controlled), metronome 60 bpm. Rest '-' or 'as needed' = rest as required, the default and most common protocol for handstands; a W:R ratio may be given (1:2 = 10 s work, 20 s rest). Handstand progress is non-linear: no session-to-session progression expectation, judge progress by skill tree milestones. Train handstand BEFORE other training (calm, focused mind, before fatiguing the nervous system). The toolkit is designed for the FLOOR (hard floor), not parallettes or mats. If a flexibility program includes shoulders or bridge, space those sessions and handstand sessions by at least 2 days.
frequency_notes: Each program states its own frequency (see programs[].frequency); 'not stated' means the sheet gives none.
Beginner 1 2.0: higher frequency = faster progress when learning to kick up and balance.
Intermediate Underbalance A/B alternate on a 5-day pattern: D1 A, D2 B, D3 off, D4 A, D5 B, D6 off, D7 repeat.
OAHS 1.0: about 2/3 weight shifting to 1/3 press over 6 days: D1 WS, D2 WS, D3 press, D4 off, D5 WS, D6 WS, D7 press/off.
OAHS 3.0 and 4.0: multiple short sessions per day suggested.
Press negatives / straddle press programs: 1 in 2 to 1 in 3 of handstand training days.
Trap raises: end of session, up to 2 x per week; a phase lasts 6 sessions.

Grease the groove (lesson 12): spread work over short bursts through the day on ONE focus drill; strength moves use reps = RM/2 with at least 15 min rest; stop if technique drops; if you cannot keep the frequency, stick to one scheduled full program.
FAQ (general, both toolkits): start at one session per week per skill and increase only once you show you recover.
Shape/line work: do not worry about the line until a 40 s freestanding hold, unless the shape causes pain (lesson 28).
rules.sides_convention: milestones[].target.sides: 'each' = must be met on each side (sheet says both sides / each side); 'both' = not side-specific or sides not stated.
